newsitem.title: USA: Clinton taps thoughtful analyst as chief economist.
newsitem.headline: Clinton taps thoughtful analyst as chief economist.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent

Janet Yellen, nominated on Friday to be President Bill Clinton's new chief economist, is a soft-spoken academic who has won the grudging respect of Wall Street during her 2 1/2 years at the Federal Reserve.

A former professor at the University of California at Berkeley, Yellen has proven to be a cautious, thoughtful policymaker at the central bank, and not the died-in-the-wool liberal than many on Wall Street feared.
"She has acquitted herself well as a Fed governor," said David Jones, vice chairman of Wall Street broker Aubrey G. Lanston and Co. "She was solid."

He said the practical policymaking experience that Yellen earned at the central bank should serve her in good stead at her new position as head of the White House's Council of Economic Advisers, which requires Senate confirmation.
In that job, the 50-year-old Yellen will act as economic sounding board for a moderate, pragmatic team of policymakers headed by Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin.
If her tenure at the Fed is any guide, she is likely to make her mark more through the thoughtfulness of her opinions than through the forcefulness of her arguments.

During her time at the central bank, Yellen was a consistent supporter of Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan -- first in his efforts to head off inflation by raising interest rates, then to keep the economy purring by cutting them.
"She came out very much in the policy mainstream," Jones said.
Equipped with a pleasant personality and an ability to laugh at herself, Yellen was well liked at the Fed but also respected for her intelligence and thoroughness.
Although her arguments tended toward the academic, Fed colleaques described her as persuasive and a voice that was listened to.
In nominating Yellen on Friday, Clinton called her an "esteemed writer and thinker who will serve our country well."
The president tapped Yellen for the job as White House chief economist after another academic, Princeton University professor Alan Blinder, turned down the position.
In accepting the nomination, Yellen said she was lucky to be nominated for the job at a time when the U.S. economy was in such good shape.

"I am very fortunate to be joining your administration at a time when the economy is in extraordinarily good health with strong job creation and low inflation," she said at a news conference with Clinton and other Cabinet appointees.
During her tenure in academia, Yellen wrote extensively in economic journals, often in collaboration with her husband, George Akerlof, himself a respected economist.
Many of her studies focused on labour markets and employment, although she also did work in such diverse fields as the East German economy and gangs and inner city crime.
Born Aug. 13, 1946 in the borough of Brooklyn in New York, Yellen graduated from Brown University in 1967 and has a doctorate in economics from Yale.
She started her career at Harvard University as assistant professor, where she taught one of the the administration's top policymakers, Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers.
After Harvard, Yellen served as an economist at the Federal Reserve Board from 1977-78, specialising in issues of international trade and finance, including stabilisation of currency rates.
After a brief tenure at the London School of Economics, Yellen joined the University of California at Berkeley in 1980.
She and her husband have one child, a son, Robert.
